title.en: History: Anti-Colonial Movements and the Birth of Nationalism

text.en: Meena read about the revolt of 1857. "Was that the first fight for freedom?" she asked.

The Revolt of 1857 began with sepoys at Meerut and spread across north and central India. Causes included greased cartridges, annexation by the Doctrine of Lapse, high taxes and loss of power for Indian rulers. Leaders were Rani Lakshmibai, Nana Sahib, Tantia Tope and Bahadur Shah Zafar.
The revolt failed due to lack of unity and British strength. After it, the rule of the Company ended and the British Crown took over in 1858.
Later the Indian National Congress was founded in 1885 by A. O. Hume and others. The early leaders, called Moderates, used petitions, and the Extremists, like Tilak, wanted bolder action. The Swadeshi movement followed the Partition of Bengal in 1905.

As the East India Company ruined weavers, imposed Zamindari and Ryotwari land taxes, and annexed kingdoms by Doctrine of Lapse, anger built across town and village.

board.text: Why resentment grew across India before 1857

text.en: Peasants and tribal communities revolted first: Bengal's Farazi and Wahhabi risings, the Kol uprising (1831–32), and Sidhu and Kanhu's Santhal Hool (1855–56).
Munda leader Birsa Munda (Ulgulan, 1899–1900) and Bengal's Indigo Revolt (1859) also exposed cruel indigo planters and forest laws.
In 1857, resentment burst into a massive uprising: on 29 March Mangal Pandey defied officers at Barrackpore, and on 10 May sepoys rebelled at Meerut.

board.text: May 1857: Meerut sepoys ignite the Great Revolt

text.en: Soldiers marched to Delhi and proclaimed elderly Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar as symbolic leader across communities.
Heroic leaders rose: Nana Sahib and Tantia Tope at Kanpur, Begum Hazrat Mahal in Awadh, Kunwar Singh in Bihar, and Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi.

board.text: 1857 heroes: Rani Lakshmibai & Begum Hazrat Mahal

text.en: Despite fierce bravery, the 1857 revolt stayed mostly north/central without coordinated national leadership or modern weapons, and was crushed by 1858.
Queen Victoria's Proclamation of November 1858 ended Company rule, brought direct Crown rule, promised religious non-interference and halted further royal annexations.
After 1858, English-educated Indians, printing presses, railways and postal links united people across languages into a shared Indian national consciousness.
In Madras, G. Subramania Iyer, M. Veeraraghavachari and others founded the Madras Mahajana Sabha (1884) and The Hindu newspaper to voice public grievances.
On 28 December 1885, 72 delegates led by first President W. C. Bonnerjee met at Bombay with retired official A. O. Hume to launch the Indian National Congress.
From 1885 to 1905, Moderates like Dadabhai Naoroji, Pherozeshah Mehta and Gopal Krishna Gokhale used petitions, speeches and reasoned debate—the '3 Ps'.
Dadabhai Naoroji—the Grand Old Man of India—exposed Britain's 'Drain of Wealth' in his book Poverty and Un-British Rule in India.
Seeing slow British replies, Extremist leaders—Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal and Lala Lajpat Rai ('Lal–Bal–Pal')—demanded bolder Swaraj.
Tilak thundered: 'Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it!' while reviving Ganapati and Shivaji festivals to rally ordinary citizens.
In 1905 Viceroy Lord Curzon split Bengal along religious lines to weaken unity—igniting the nationwide Swadeshi and Boycott movement.
People burned foreign cloth, sang Bankim's Vande Mataram, started Swadeshi banks and national schools, and saw V. O. Chidambaram Pillai launch Indian steamships in Tamil Nadu.

board.text: Swadeshi boycott & V.O.C.'s ships in TN

text.en: At the 1907 Surat Session, Moderates and Extremists split temporarily, while the 1906 Muslim League formed at Dhaka and revolutionary groups grew secretly.
Yet unity returned cleanly in 1916: Annie Besant in Madras and Tilak in Pune launched Home Rule Leagues, signing the historic 1916 Lucknow Pact.
Notice the clear progression cleanly: scattered tribal/1857 revolts -> organised Moderate critique -> mass Swadeshi boycott -> Home Rule self-government demand.
To trace the big story: economic exploitation + printing press -> 1885 INC voice -> 1905 Partition challenge -> united national awakening.
By 1916, Indians from Madras to Bengal and Punjab were ready for nationwide mass Satyagraha under Mahatma Gandhi.

board.text: Foundation set for nationwide freedom struggle

problem.en: How did Dadabhai Naoroji's 'Drain of Wealth' theory change how Indians viewed British rule?

text.en: Look before 1885.

why.en: Many educated Indians initially believed British rule brought modern law and progress.

text.en: Examine Naoroji's evidence.

why.en: In his book and speeches, Naoroji showed Indian taxes funded British salaries, army wars abroad, and raw cotton exports while peasants starved.

text.en: Connect to nationalism.

why.en: Once people saw poverty was man-made under colonial rule, Moderates, Swadeshi leaders and later mass movements demanded Indian control of India's economy.

prompt.en: A friend says The Indian National Congress was founded in 1857. How will you reply?

points.en: Swadeshi after the Partition of Bengal.
